abstract: Summary Renal fibrosis (RF) is the main pathological feature and a potential therapeutic target of chronic kidney disease (CKD), a prevalent health problem causing a high economic burden to the health care system. Fat mass and obesity-associated (FTO) inhibition, either genetically or pharmacologically, significantly reduced collagen deposition, lipid peroxidation, and ferroptosis marker expression after unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) compared with sham-operated controls in mice. In murine and human kidney epithelial cells as well as in human embryonic stem cell-derived kidney organoids, FTO inhibition reduced erastin-induced ferroptosis by decreasing lipid peroxidation and reactive oxygen species production by downregulating the ferroptosis driver ACSL4. Moreover, FTO inhibition directly downregulated TGFBI, which was strongly associated with reduced M2 macrophage accumulation after UUO. Our results provide a strong rationale for targeting FTO to alleviate RF in patients subjected to obstruction-related kidney injury, thereby reducing the prevalence of CKD and associated treatment costs and improving the quality of life.

Experimental model and study participant details
Mouse UUO model
All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Stanford University. C57/BL6 female mice aged 8–12 weeks were housed in a specific pathogen-free environment within the Animal Care Facility of Stanford University. All experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Stanford University (Protocol No. 30864). We surgically induced UUO by applying a nontraumatic microvascular clamp on the left ureter in these mice as previously described.
27
Sham-operated mice underwent laparotomy and ureteral mobilization without clamping. Left kidneys were harvested 14 days after obstruction. They were bisected and one half was fixed in formalin overnight for subsequent sectioning and the other half was frozen quickly on crushed dry ice before being transferred to a −80°C freezer for RNA and protein isolation. Blood from UUO and control mice was also collected at the end of the experiment.
Therapeutic treatment of mice
WT 6–8-week-old female mice that had undergone surgically induced UUO were randomized based on weight into 3 groups (n=6/group) and treated with either vehicle, FB23-2, a potent FTO-specific inhibitor, or Lipro-1, an effective ferroptosis inhibitor, via daily intraperitoneal injection for 14 days. SOC treated with the vehicle was used as control. A total of 24 mice were used. The number of mice used was determined based on a pilot study showing a near-significant difference with the same treatments using three mice per group. All mice were included in the analysis since no mouse experienced weight loss >=20% which was the exclusion criteria set
a priori
. All mice were housed in the same location (room and rack) and treated at the same time each day to minimize variations.
Conditional FTO KO model
Female mice with conditional KO of the FTO gene in kidney tubule cells were generated through the crossing of KSP-1 Cre mice (Strain #:012237, The Jackson Laboratory) with FTO-Loxp mice (Strain #:034855, The Jackson Laboratory). Genotyping was done by PCR.
Cell culture and treatment
Primary renal epithelial cells were generated from kidney tissues excised from
8- to 12-wk-old C57/BL6 female mice and cultured
in Renal Epithelial Cell Growth Medium 2 (PromoCell C-26030) as previously described.
27
HK2 cells were purchased from ATCC and cultured in DMEM/F12 supplemented with 10% FBS. For treatments, cells were seeded in 96-well plates in 200 μL medium and treated with 1 μM erastin, 5 μM Lipro-1 or 2 μM FB23-2 for 24 hours. Cell viability was determined using a Cell Titer Glo kit (Promega G9242).
Generation of human embryonic stem cell (hESC)-derived kidney organoids
hESC H1 cells (gift from Dr. Ang at Stanford University) authenticated and free of mycoplasma infection, were used to generate kidney organoids by applying an established kidney organoid production protocol with modification.
62
,
63
Briefly, at 40-50% confluency, H1 cells cultured in mTeSR medium (Stem Cell Technologies) and Matrigel-coated culture dishes (Corning) were differentiated into metanephric mesenchyme cells which include nephron progenitor cells by treatment with 8 μM GSK-3 inhibitor CHIR99021 (to Day 4, R&D) followed by 200 ng/mL FGF9 induction (to Day 9, PeproTech). Metanephric mesenchyme cells were then be transferred into suspension culture in 6-well ultra-low attachment plates and further differentiated into kidney organoids through intermediate stages of peritubular aggregates (day 11) and renal vesicles (day 14).
Generation of FTO KO cells by CRISPR-Gas9. FTO KO HK2 and hESC cells were generated using CRISPR-Cas9 system. Three sgFTO sequences were used (Target1: CGGGACCTGGTTAGGATCCA; Target2: CCTACAAGTACCTGAACACC Target3: CCAGGCTCTTTACGGTCCCC) (ABM Goods Inc). The dCas9 construct was obtained from Addgene.
100
All lentiviruses were generated using a third-generation system. Briefly, 293T cells were cultured in the presence of chloroquine diphosphate at a final concentration of 50 μM for 5 hours. Lentiviral constructs (17 μg) were mixed with pMDL(11 μg), VSV-G (6 μg), and pREV (4 μg) in HEPES buffered saline with CaCl2 at a final concentration of 0.5M, and the resulting DNA-calcium phosphate co-precipitate was added onto 293T cells. After incubating overnight, the medium was removed and replenished. Two days later, medium containing lentiviruses was collected and concentrated using a PEG-it kit (LV810A-1, System Biosciences). HK2 cells were transduced with dCas9 lentiviral particles in medium containing polybrene at a concentration of 8 μg/mL for 3 days. Lentiviral particles carrying pX333 plasmids containing the FTO guide RNAs were then transduced into HK2 and hESC cells expressing dCas9.

Collagen level determination by sirius red staining and hydroxyproline assay
Collagen deposition in mouse kidney tissues was determined by Sirius red staining using a Picro Sirius Red Stain Kit according to manufacturer’s instructions (Abcam: ab150681). Briefly, 5-micron-thick formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded sections were deparaffinized and hydrated in distilled water before Picro Sirius Red Solution was applied to completely cover the tissue section and incubated for 60 minutes. Sections were then rinsed quickly in 2 changes of acetic acid solution and dehydrated in absolute alcohol. Sections were then mounted and visualized under a standard light microscope. Hydroxyproline from mouse kidney tissues was quantified using a modified assay based on hydrochloric acid (HCl) in Ehrlich's solution as previously described.

After baking at 110°C overnight in HCl, samples were reconstituted in water, and hydroxyproline content was measured using a colorimetric chloramine T assay (Sigma MAK008).
Malondialdehyde (MDA) assay
MDA levels were quantified through a controlled reaction using a thiobarbituric acid kit (TBARS (TCA Method) Assay Kit, Cayman: Item No. 700870) according to the manufacturer’s guidelines. Briefly, 25 mg of tissues or 20 million cells were homogenized in 250 μl RIPA lysis buffer and mixed with 100 μl of TCA Assay Reagent and 800 μl of the color Reagent. After the reaction was complete, the absorbance was measured at 535 nm. RIPA lysis buffer without tissues or cells was used as a control. All samples were evaluated in triplicates. MDA levels from each sample were calculated from a standard curve.

Introduction
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) caused by acute kidney injury (AKI) due to infection, toxic chemicals, ischemia-reperfusion, kidney obstruction, and lifestyle-related diseases such as diabetes is a prevalent health problem causing a high economic burden to the health care system.
1
,
2
It has risen from the 18
th
cause of loss of years of full health in 2010 to the 10
th
in 2019
3
and is projected to become the fifth global cause of death by 2040.
4
Currently, there are no targeted therapies that can prevent or reverse kidney damage caused by the main risk factors of CKD.
5
Therapeutic strategies that can effectively block or attenuate kidney damage leading to CKD are urgently needed to decrease the mortality rate, improve the quality of life, and reduce the economic burden on CKD patients.
Renal fibrosis (RF) is characterized by the production of excessive extracellular matrix, such as collagen deposited in the tubulointerstitial space and glomerulus area, ultimately leading to the destruction of renal parenchyma and loss of renal function.
6
It is the main pathological feature of CDK, irrespective of the initial injury, and a potential therapeutic target of CKD.
7
Antifibrotic agents shown to reduce fibrosis in other organs are being tested in CKD clinical trials.
8
,
9
Ferroptosis, a regulated cell death mechanism characterized by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production,
10
has been associated with the development of RF in several mouse models, such as unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) and ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI)-induced AKI models.
11
,
12
The therapeutic potential of ferroptosis inhibitors in RF has been a recent focus in CKD management.
13
In addition, strong correlations have been found between the presence of M2 macrophages and progressive fibrosis in several human diseases, including systemic sclerosis,
14
pulmonary fibrosis,
15
,
16
ovarian fibrosis,
17
and liver fibrosis.
18
In the kidney, an increased prevalence of M2 macrophages was observed in diverse animal models of RF and CDK patient samples, suggesting that M2 macrophages play a pivotal role in fibrogenesis within the kidney.
19
,
20
The fat mass and obesity-associated (FTO) protein, an m
6
A RNA demethylase that plays an important role in various human diseases such as obesity and cancer,
21
may promote UUO-induced RF in mice. Specifically, FTO expression increases after UUO, and FTO deficiency attenuates the fibrogenic responses induced by UUO.
22
,
23
,
24
,
25
We previously reported that FTO upregulates glutamine transporter SLC1A5, a ferroptosis activator, in VHL-deficient clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) cells,
26
suggesting that FTO promotes ferroptosis in ccRCC cells. In addition, we found that ROS production was upregulated after UUO in mice, consistent with a promoting role of ferroptosis in RF.
27
In this study, we determined the effects of genetic or pharmacological inhibition of FTO on ferroptosis and UUO-induced RF using multiple pre-clinical models. Moreover, we identified molecular targets of FTO, including the ferroptosis activator ACSL4
28
and profibrotic macrophage inducer TGF-induced protein (TGFBI),
29
that reveal the underlying mechanisms of FTO action in RF.

We previously performed gene expression profiling on mouse kidneys after UUO over a time course of 7 days.
30
Here, we determined whether the 501 ferroptosis-associated genes (drivers, suppressors, and markers) annotated in FerrDb,
31
,
32
a manually curated ferroptosis database, were enriched in differentially expressed genes that we previously identified between sham-operated control (SOC) vs. UUO tissues by gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) analysis. Enrichment was first observed at 5 h after UUO initiation and persisted for 3 days, with the greatest enrichment at 12 h based on normalized enrichment score, nominal
p
value, and false discovery rate
q
value (
Figure 1
A). Of the core genes identified by GSEA that contributed the most to the enrichment at each time point, 75 were found in at least two of the five time points (5 h, 7 h, 12 h, 1 day, and 3 days) (
Table S1
). Supervised hierarchical clustering of these genes demonstrated that a subset of known ferroptosis drivers was significantly upregulated at the early time points (5–12 h) including the
ATF4-CHAC1
pathway,

,

whereas other genes such as

and

Discussion
Our study identified FTO as a key mediator of UUO-induced RF by promoting ferroptosis and profibrotic M2 macrophage populations. Inhibition of FTO, either pharmacologically or genetically, protects against UUO-induced RF by directly downregulating ACSL4 and TGFBI, two vital genes driving ferroptosis and upregulating M2 macrophage accumulation, respectively, at the transcript level by modulating m
6
A methylation. Our study employed multiple
in vitro
and
in vivo
models to elucidate the role of FTO in ferroptosis and RF, including a highly realistic hESC-derived kidney organoid model, therefore providing a strong rationale for targeting FTO as a therapeutic strategy to alleviate RF in patients at risk for obstruction-related kidney injury. Given the important clinical applications that effective FTO inhibitors could have in human diseases, great efforts have been made to identify and develop selective FTO inhibitors in the past years, such as small molecule inhibitor CS1 and PROTAC degrader QP73.
64
,
65
Our results will accelerate the clinical testing of these FTO inhibitors not only in RF but also potentially in other fibrotic diseases.
Several studies have implicated FTO in ferroptosis in various cell types after acute injury. For example, FTO overexpression impairs dihydroartemisinin-induced ferroptosis in hepatic stellate cells and alleviates liver fibrosis in mice,
66
,
67
indicating an inhibitory role of FTO in dihydroartemisinin-induced ferroptosis in liver cells. In contrast, arbutin, a natural antioxidant, inhibits the onset of ferroptosis and ameliorates high-fat-diet-induced liver fibrosis
in vivo
by downregulating FTO and its target SLC7A11, a known ferroptosis driver, suggesting a promoting role of FTO in high-fat-diet-induced liver fibrosis.
68
However, in brain cells, FTO knockdown increased the infarct size of brain tissues and neuronal damage in ischemic stroke by promoting ferroptosis,
69
suggesting a protective role of FTO in neuronal cell ferroptosis. The cell type-specific role of FTO in ferroptosis may be due to the differential impact of m
6
A modification on the expression of different, or sometimes even the same, ferroptosis regulators in different cell types. For example, in kidney epithelial cells, FTO inhibition increased m
6
A modification in ACSL4 transcripts, resulting in reduced transcript level and protein expression of ACSL4, whereas in a mouse model of ischemic stroke, FTO upregulation decreased m
6
A level in ACSL4 transcript and also reduced ACSL4 protein expression.
69
It seems that the balance between the positive and negative impact of m
6
A modification on ACSL4 transcript levels in different cell types determines the net up- or downregulation of ACSL4 protein expression and the effects of FTO on ferroptosis in different cell types.
70
Several recent studies suggest that FTO upregulation suppresses ferroptosis by downregulating ferroptosis drivers such as ACSL4 and TFRC or upregulating ferroptosis suppressors such as GPX4, SLC7A11, and NRF2 in colorectal cancer, liver IRI, doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity, and lipopolysaccharide-induced acute lung injury.
71
,
72
,
73
,
74
However, a number of reports demonstrate a promoting role of FTO in ferroptosis by downregulating GPX4, NRF2, SLC7A11, and ACSL3 in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, Parkinson disease, oral squamous cell carcinoma, and thyroid cancer.
75
,
76
,
77
,
78
High FTO and ferroptosis are also associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and diabetic cataracts.
79
,
80
Therefore, there is abundant literature documenting that FTO can promote or attenuate ferroptosis depending on several factors including cell type, tissue type, specific injuries, and interventions. These results indicate that the role of FTO in ferroptosis is highly context dependent.
Mechanistically, FTO can up- or downregulate different ferroptosis drivers/suppressors or even the same ferroptosis regulator in a context-dependent manner. For instance, FTO promotes GPX4 expression in colorectal cancer and ischemic stroke while inhibiting GPX4 expression in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
69
,
72
,
77
Similarly, FTO enhances NRF2 expression to alleviate doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity while impairing NRF2 expression to promote ferroptosis in Parkinson disease.
73
,
78
Interestingly, FTO regulates the expression of these ferroptosis suppressors by reducing the m
6
A level of their transcripts, suggesting that decreased m
6
A level in the transcripts of these genes may confer either increased or decreased protein expression. Alternatively, FTO may regulate the m
6
A level of other proteins, such as BAP1 and MDM2, which indirectly affect the expression of SLC7A11 in Parkinson disease and
Staphylococcus aureus
-induced osteomyelitis, respectively.
75
,
81
The mechanism by which FTO regulates ACSL4 expression is still under investigation. Jin et al. demonstrated that FTO knockdown increased the m
6
A level in ACSL4 transcript, which was recognized by the m
6
A reader YTHDF3, leading to increased ACSL4 mRNA stability and protein expression in ischemic stroke-induced neuronal injury.
69
Similarly, FTO deficiency in older livers exacerbates ferroptosis during IRI by upregulating the m
6
A level in ACSL4 transcript recognized by the m
6
A reader YTHDC2, resulting in increased ACSL4 mRNA stability and protein expression,
71
although in hepatic fibrosis, the m
6
A reader YTHDF2 promoted ACSL4 transcript stability and protein expression by recognizing m
6
A.
82
Consistently, in our study, FTO knockdown increased the m
6
A level in ACSL4 transcript; however, it led to a decreased ACSL4 protein expression through an unknown mechanism, suggesting that increased m
6
A level in ACSL4 transcript may confer either increased or decreased protein expression as described above for GPX4 and NRF2. These findings underscore the complexity of ferroptosis regulation by FTO in diverse cell types through key components of the pathway.
FTO is expressed by M2 macrophages, and FTO knockdown suppresses M2 macrophage polarization in mice,
83
suggesting that FTO directly regulates M2 macrophage abundance in mice. However, our data strongly suggest that reduced M2 macrophage infiltration is largely due to the downregulation of TGFBI in an m
6
A-dependent manner. Since FTO KO is epithelial cell specific in the mouse kidneys, this rules out the possibility that the reduction in M2 macrophage infiltration in FTO knockdown mice is due to a loss of function of FTO in macrophages. CD206/MCR1
+
M2 profibrotic macrophages have been shown to augment fibrosis in both human and experimental diseases.
84
,
85
,
86
TGFBI, ubiquitously detected in normal human tissues including the kidney, has been associated with several diseases such as fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis, and diabetic kidney disease, as well as an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in cancer, partly attributed to its promoting role in monocyte chemotaxis and M2 macrophage differentiation.
29
,
87
,
88
Our results revealed a strong association between TGFBI transcript and protein levels with the expression of profibrotic CD206/MRC1
+
CD163
+
M2 macrophage markers in UUO kidney tissues. This may explain the superior protective effects of FTO inhibitor FB23-2 on UUO-induced RF compared with the ferroptosis inhibitor Lipro-1. Additional FTO-regulated molecular targets and cellular processes implicated in UUO-induced RF include SQSTM1 in autophagy,
41
TASK-2 in cell cycle,
24
and TGF-β1/RUNX1 and lncRNA GAS5 in epithelial-mesenchymal transition.
23
,
25
These observations provided a strong rationale for developing FTO-targeted therapeutics to combat RF from multiple fronts.
Kidney organoids derived from hESCs contain segmented structures with podocytes, proximal tubules, and distal tubules in nephron-like arrangements that recapitulate kidney development and enable the modeling of complex kidney diseases.
60
,
89
,
90
In particular, kidney organoids have served as an
in vitro
platform to elucidate mechanisms of AKI and RF with great success.
59
,
91
Recently, it has been reported that orthotopic transplantation under the kidney capsule enables the generation of kidney organoid xenografts with improved anatomic maturity and vascularization, making them the most clinically relevant
in vivo
models for elucidating molecular mechanisms driving kidney diseases and for the development of pharmacotherapies.
92
,
93
,
94
In the future, we will investigate the effects of FTO inhibition on ferroptosis and RF using organoid-derived xenografts
in vivo
to facilitate the clinical translation of our results to patient care.
Limitations of the study
Several additional investigations are needed to address the limitations of our study. First, single-cell RNA sequencing could be performed to confirm the kidney tubule cell-specific knockdown of FTO and the cellular source of FTO upregulation. Second, the role of FTO in AKI and RF could be evaluated in additional acute kidney injuries, such as ischemia-reperfusion. Third, whether FTO expression is correlated with RF in human kidney tissues needs further validation. Finally, more potent and specific FTO inhibitors than FB23-2 are needed for FTO-targeted therapy to ameliorate AKI-induced RF.

Experimental model and study participant details
Mouse UUO model
All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Stanford University. C57/BL6 female mice aged 8–12 weeks were housed in a specific pathogen-free environment within the Animal Care Facility of Stanford University. All experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Stanford University (Protocol No. 30864). We surgically induced UUO by applying a nontraumatic microvascular clamp on the left ureter in these mice as previously described.
27
Sham-operated mice underwent laparotomy and ureteral mobilization without clamping. Left kidneys were harvested 14 days after obstruction. They were bisected and one half was fixed in formalin overnight for subsequent sectioning and the other half was frozen quickly on crushed dry ice before being transferred to a −80°C freezer for RNA and protein isolation. Blood from UUO and control mice was also collected at the end of the experiment.
Therapeutic treatment of mice
WT 6–8-week-old female mice that had undergone surgically induced UUO were randomized based on weight into 3 groups (n=6/group) and treated with either vehicle, FB23-2, a potent FTO-specific inhibitor, or Lipro-1, an effective ferroptosis inhibitor, via daily intraperitoneal injection for 14 days. SOC treated with the vehicle was used as control. A total of 24 mice were used. The number of mice used was determined based on a pilot study showing a near-significant difference with the same treatments using three mice per group. All mice were included in the analysis since no mouse experienced weight loss >=20% which was the exclusion criteria set
a priori
. All mice were housed in the same location (room and rack) and treated at the same time each day to minimize variations.
Conditional FTO KO model
Female mice with conditional KO of the FTO gene in kidney tubule cells were generated through the crossing of KSP-1 Cre mice (Strain #:012237, The Jackson Laboratory) with FTO-Loxp mice (Strain #:034855, The Jackson Laboratory). Genotyping was done by PCR.
Cell culture and treatment
Primary renal epithelial cells were generated from kidney tissues excised from
8- to 12-wk-old C57/BL6 female mice and cultured
in Renal Epithelial Cell Growth Medium 2 (PromoCell C-26030) as previously described.
27
HK2 cells were purchased from ATCC and cultured in DMEM/F12 supplemented with 10% FBS. For treatments, cells were seeded in 96-well plates in 200 μL medium and treated with 1 μM erastin, 5 μM Lipro-1 or 2 μM FB23-2 for 24 hours. Cell viability was determined using a Cell Titer Glo kit (Promega G9242).
Generation of human embryonic stem cell (hESC)-derived kidney organoids
hESC H1 cells (gift from Dr. Ang at Stanford University) authenticated and free of mycoplasma infection, were used to generate kidney organoids by applying an established kidney organoid production protocol with modification.
62
,
63
Briefly, at 40-50% confluency, H1 cells cultured in mTeSR medium (Stem Cell Technologies) and Matrigel-coated culture dishes (Corning) were differentiated into metanephric mesenchyme cells which include nephron progenitor cells by treatment with 8 μM GSK-3 inhibitor CHIR99021 (to Day 4, R&D) followed by 200 ng/mL FGF9 induction (to Day 9, PeproTech). Metanephric mesenchyme cells were then be transferred into suspension culture in 6-well ultra-low attachment plates and further differentiated into kidney organoids through intermediate stages of peritubular aggregates (day 11) and renal vesicles (day 14).
Generation of FTO KO cells by CRISPR-Gas9. FTO KO HK2 and hESC cells were generated using CRISPR-Cas9 system. Three sgFTO sequences were used (Target1: CGGGACCTGGTTAGGATCCA; Target2: CCTACAAGTACCTGAACACC Target3: CCAGGCTCTTTACGGTCCCC) (ABM Goods Inc). The dCas9 construct was obtained from Addgene.
100
All lentiviruses were generated using a third-generation system. Briefly, 293T cells were cultured in the presence of chloroquine diphosphate at a final concentration of 50 μM for 5 hours. Lentiviral constructs (17 μg) were mixed with pMDL(11 μg), VSV-G (6 μg), and pREV (4 μg) in HEPES buffered saline with CaCl2 at a final concentration of 0.5M, and the resulting DNA-calcium phosphate co-precipitate was added onto 293T cells. After incubating overnight, the medium was removed and replenished. Two days later, medium containing lentiviruses was collected and concentrated using a PEG-it kit (LV810A-1, System Biosciences). HK2 cells were transduced with dCas9 lentiviral particles in medium containing polybrene at a concentration of 8 μg/mL for 3 days. Lentiviral particles carrying pX333 plasmids containing the FTO guide RNAs were then transduced into HK2 and hESC cells expressing dCas9.
Method details
Western blot
Total protein extraction was performed on frozen kidney tissues or cultured cells using RIPA lysis buffer (10mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0+1mM EDTA+0.5mM EGTA+1% Triton X-100+0.1% Sodium Deoxycholate+0.1% SDS+140mM NaCl) containing protease inhibitors. Immunoblot analysis was conducted using the following antibodies according to standard techniques as previously described.
26
Proteomic profiling by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS)
Proteomic profiling in HK2 cells was performed using an Orbitrap Tribrid Eclipse mass spectrometer, equipped with an Orbitrap mass analyzer as previously described.
101
,
102
Briefly, proteins were extracted using a lysis buffer containing 12.5 mM Tris pH 8.0 (Fisher Scientific), 0.5 mM EDTA (EMD Inc.), 7.5 M urea (Sigma-Aldrich), and 1× protease inhibitor and protein concentrations were determined by BCA protein assay according to manufacturer’s instruction (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). 25 μg of protein were reduced, alkylated, and digested with trypsin (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The resulting tryptic peptides were reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid (50 μl, Fisher Scientific) and fractionated using a Dionex Ultimate Rapid Separation liquid chromatography system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) before being analyzed on an Orbitrap Tribrid Eclipse mass spectrometer, equipped with an Orbitrap mass analyzer. Unprocessed data are available via ProteomeXchange with the identifier PXD051362.
Proteomic data analysis
Following LC-MS analysis, the raw data collected for each cell line was searched using Byonic 4.0.12 against the Swiss-Prot human database (2022, 20644 entries), including 10 ppm of precursor tolerance, and 0.5 Da for fragment tolerance along with fixed carbamidomethyl cysteine, variable methionine oxidation, and deamidated asparagine, and allowing up to two missed cleavages. Peptides with a false discovery rate (FDR) greater than 1% were excluded. Then we perform a relative quantification at the peptide level to integrate them into protein quantification using a weighted average and adjusting each sample protein quantification to a normal distribution of average 0 and standard deviation of 1
N(0,1)
. Statistical significance was assessed using the Student's T-test, with a stringent cutoff set at a p-value of less than 0.01 to identify proteins of interest for further analysis.
Lipidomic profiling by LC-MS
This assay was performed at UCLA Lipidomic Core as previously described.
103
Specifically, the assay was built on the Sciex Lipidyzer Platform which employed a SCIEX 5500 triple-quadrupole (QQQ) with a Shimadzu auto-sampler configured for direct infusion experiments, SelexION ion mobility device, and Shimadzu LC. An in-house data analysis workflow utilizing the mathematical modeling-based isotopic spectral analysis and a combination of 70 lipid standards sourced from Sciex and Avanti Polar Lipids were used to provide accurate, quantitative measurements of over 1400 lipid species across 17 lipid subclasses within a biological sample.

Collagen level determination by sirius red staining and hydroxyproline assay
Collagen deposition in mouse kidney tissues was determined by Sirius red staining using a Picro Sirius Red Stain Kit according to manufacturer’s instructions (Abcam: ab150681). Briefly, 5-micron-thick formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded sections were deparaffinized and hydrated in distilled water before Picro Sirius Red Solution was applied to completely cover the tissue section and incubated for 60 minutes. Sections were then rinsed quickly in 2 changes of acetic acid solution and dehydrated in absolute alcohol. Sections were then mounted and visualized under a standard light microscope. Hydroxyproline from mouse kidney tissues was quantified using a modified assay based on hydrochloric acid (HCl) in Ehrlich's solution as previously described.
27
Briefly, kidney tissues were homogenized in 1 mL water for 30 s using a handheld homogenizer, and solid components were precipitated with trichloroacetic acid. After baking at 110°C overnight in HCl, samples were reconstituted in water, and hydroxyproline content was measured using a colorimetric chloramine T assay (Sigma MAK008).
Malondialdehyde (MDA) assay
MDA levels were quantified through a controlled reaction using a thiobarbituric acid kit (TBARS (TCA Method) Assay Kit, Cayman: Item No. 700870) according to the manufacturer’s guidelines. Briefly, 25 mg of tissues or 20 million cells were homogenized in 250 μl RIPA lysis buffer and mixed with 100 μl of TCA Assay Reagent and 800 μl of the color Reagent. After the reaction was complete, the absorbance was measured at 535 nm. RIPA lysis buffer without tissues or cells was used as a control. All samples were evaluated in triplicates. MDA levels from each sample were calculated from a standard curve.
